newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan parliament adopts '97/98 government budget.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan parliament adopts '97/98 government budget.

text.p: Taiwan's parliament has approved the government's 1997/98 budget that pours new funds into public works and fortifies the island against rival China.
The Legislative Yuan late on Friday adopted the Nationalist government's spending proposal, but whittled away T$18.2 billion (US$654 million) -- including T$3.1 billion in proposed defence spending.
The final approval authorises spending of T$1.2253 trillion, a 4.1 percent rise over 1996/97.
Defence, as always, is the biggest area of spending -- a reflection of Taiwan's nearly half-century rivalry with the communist People's Republic of China across the Taiwan Strait.

The biggest increase goes to a special public-works budget dubbed "economic development", up 12.4 percent in a reflection of the Nationalist government's goal of nuturing a slowly gathering economic recovery.
Defence spending, budgeted separately from the main plan, rises three percent to T$257.1 billion, equivalent to one-fifth of the total non-defence budget.
The budget includes a special T$47.4 billion budget for the purchase of advanced French and U.S. warplanes, part of a nine-year T$300.7 billion fighter procurement fund.

Taiwan says it needs the 60 Mirage and 150 F16 fighters to counter a steady modernisation of China's three-million strong People's Liberation Army, which put its growing military clout on dramatic display during eight months of war games and missile tests near Taiwan in 1995 and 1996.

Beijing said it mounted the manoeuvres to chill any ideas of establishing an independent Taiwan, especially as the island went to the polls in March 1996 for the first popular presidential election in Chinese history.
Yet despite its increase in dollar terms, the defence budget actually shrinks by 0.2 percentage points relative to the total budget, slipping to 20.9 percent from 21.1 percent.
Such was not the case for the economic development portion of the budget, which swells to T$132.3 billion, or 10.6 percent, of total spending, up 0.8 percentage points from a year ago.
The category includes all but the biggest infrastructure projects such as superhighways and the high-speed railway.
The budget plans for a deficit of about T$100 billion, down an annual 40 percent. ($1 = 27.85)
